source.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Kyle O'Brien; D. Majercak; Xavier Fernandes; Richard Edgar; Jingya Chen; Harsha Nori; Dean Carignan; Eric Horvitz; F. Poursabzi-Sangdeh

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or truncation; the supplied text includes the paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE feature identification and steering to real language models and reports results bearing on the claim that LLMs contain sparse features recoverable by an SAE. It does not test the original toy-model superposition claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many SAE-steering results. Rows below retain results most directly relevant to whether SAE features can be identified and have behavioral effects. Benchmark accuracy, safe-prompt refusal, alternative steering methods, and most detailed Llama clamp sweeps are not recorded as separate rows because they do not directly measure the recoverability claim. The reported grid search identifies candidate features; its results are not cited from other work.
record.test_reason: The study uses a Top-k SAE on Phi-3 Mini and Llama 3.1 8B as a tool. It picks features from one refusal response and clamps them to steer refusal. All results are rates for its own steering method (refusals, attack success, benchmark accuracy), compared with prompting and PASTA. It never asks whether LLM representations are superposed or whether the SAE recovers the model's sparse features. It reports no feature-recovery, interpretability, completeness or stability measure, so it bears on none of V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Amplifying SAE refusal features improves single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak robustness. It also causes over-refusal and broad drops on MMLU, TruthfulQA and GSM8K, even where no refusal occurs. The authors add that the philosophy-feature ablation shows these regressions are a general limitation of feature steering, not specific to safety features. They also say refusal features may be entangled with general capabilities.
record.recipe_differences: This is an application of SAE feature identification and activation clamping to refusal steering in pretrained LMs, not the toy-network feature-superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with the feature and clamp value; the authors report different outcomes for Features 22373 and 20528, and for the two Llama features. The selected SAE layer is layer 6; the authors state that layer 6 had substantially better training performance than the other layers they studied.

fits_no_version.finding: Clamping a single SAE feature degrades unrelated capabilities: MMLU 68.8%→36.0%, GSM8K 82.5%→35.6% at clamp 12. A philosophy feature (216) degrades accuracy similarly. The authors read this as suggesting a lack of modularity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering individual SAE features in LLMs produces broad off-target effects, suggesting those features are not cleanly isolated units.

fits_no_version.finding: Several SAE features (22373, 20528, and others in Table 7) each raise refusal when amplified. The authors infer that refusal is not mediated by a single feature.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single behaviour can be mediated by multiple distinct SAE features.

record.problems: The main analysis is on Phi-3 Mini with one SAE architecture and a selected layer; the Llama experiment is described as initial. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated results. Crescendo uses an automated attacker and judge setup that the authors say may change as the implementation develops. Feature identification begins from a single archetypal refusal response, and the authors state that feature interactions and monosemanticity remain open questions.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-clamp results for Llama in Table 12, other safety and capability measures in Tables 1-3, 6, 8, 12, 15 and 16, and additional attack results in Tables 4-5 are omitted; they report further steering effects, but do not add distinct evidence about SAE feature recoverability beyond the retained results.

untested.parts: All: no capacity or polysemanticity analysis.
Whether features are spread across neurons, and whether the SAE recovers the model's sparse features; no recovery or interpretability metric is reported.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not measured.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests V4 / supports' should be overturned. The study assumes SAE features exist and reports only how well its steering performs, so it is T4. None of its rows bears on any superposition version.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions; overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity arises from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.

The study tests whether SAE-derived sparse features in real LMs can be identified and behaviorally steered. It does not test whether features are spread across many neurons, or directly measure how many neurons encode each feature.
The study does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
The study does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Phi-3 Mini and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, under the reported feature-clamping settings
reader_labels.reason: The authors identify SAE features and report that amplifying them changes refusal behavior on Wild Guard and Crescendo; a second model also shows this pattern (r1, r2, r5-r8, r10-r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: XSTest unsafe prompts and Crescendo Pay at clamp 10
reader_labels.reason: The authors report no meaningful XSTest improvement, and Pay attack success rises at clamp 10 rather than falling (r3, r4, r9).
